raw_response.country: Multi-country (global cross-country averages from Global Water Intelligence and World Bank IBNET databases; exact country list and sample sizes not reported)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines municipal water and sanitation service access conceptually across three urban development phases and presents descriptive country-level averages for urban piped water coverage and urban sewer connection coverage (Figures 1 and 2).
criterion_notes.c2: Under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper conceptually discusses tariff and cost-recovery rules governing service access (increasing block tariffs, lifeline subsidies, full-cost recovery pricing and Customer Assistance Programs), alongside broader regulatory incentives and informal 'shadow state' governance. However, these rule-type mechanisms are examined only in a narrative conceptual/policy overview (Sections 2 and 4); in Section 3's descriptive cross-country scatterplots, service-access outcomes (Figures 1-3) are plotted solely against national GDP per capita (macroeconomic income, which fails both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2 as an exposure), while tariff and cost-recovery indicators (OCCR, revenue per m3 and price for 15 m3 in Figures 4-6) are plotted solely against GDP per capita and physical water stress, never against service access. Consequently, the paper is excluded under both the narrow rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
criterion_notes.c3: Excluded as E05: the paper is a conceptual framework and policy perspective Letter proposing three stylized phases of municipal WASH development and a four-part policy mix for the Anthropocene, with no empirical methods section, no primary data and no systematic empirical synthesis. Although Section 3 includes six illustrative bivariate scatterplots from secondary databases (GWI and IBNET) and one correlation coefficient between water stress and residential water prices, it reports no sample sizes, selection criteria or empirical method testing how any legal, administrative, regulatory or tariff mechanism affects service access.
criterion_notes.c4: Describes country-level urban piped water coverage and urban sewer connection coverage in Figures 1 and 2 (plotted only against GDP per capita), while Figures 4-6 plot utility financial and price metrics without linking them to household access, connection, reliability, affordability or exclusion outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not provide an identifiable empirical study design linking a population, a legal/regulatory/tariff exposure and a service-access outcome; exact country and utility sample sizes in the IBNET and GWI scatterplots are not reported in the text, and the access plots examine only GDP per capita rather than a legal or tariff exposure.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper describes three phases that cities go through for the delivery of municipal water and sanitation services, identifying the main political, technological, socio-institutional, financial, public health forces of disequilibria that push cities along this development path.

Data from the Global Water Intelligence and the World Bank’s International Benchmarking Network show that most of the countries with utilities with limited piped water coverage (Phase 1) have an annual GDP per capita less than US$5000.
States thus deploy different pricing and subsidy policies in each of the three phases.
These higher tariffs typically require that the state establishes Customer Assistance Programs (CAPs) to ensure that services are affordable to poor households
Figures 2 and 3 show country-level averages for urban population with sewer connections versus annual GDP per capita and urban population with treated wastewater versus GDP per capita
Figure 6 compares the average price of water that residential customers pay for 15 m3 per month with a country-level water stress indicator.

raw_response.exposure: Narrative overview discusses tariff and subsidy policies (increasing block tariffs, cost recovery, Customer Assistance Programs), regulatory incentives and shadow-state governance; descriptive cross-country plots examine annual GDP per capita (Figures 1-5) and country-level water stress (Figure 6).
raw_response.outcome: Country-level urban piped water coverage (Figure 1), urban sewer connection coverage (Figure 2), treated wastewater coverage (Figure 3), utility operating cost coverage ratio (Figure 4), average revenue per cubic meter sold (Figure 5) and average residential price of water for 15 m3 per month (Figure 6).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Country-level municipal water utility averages drawn from the Global Water Intelligence (GWI) database and the World Bank's International Benchmarking Network (IBNET) (exact number of countries and utilities not reported).
raw_response.rationale: This Environmental Research Letters article is a conceptual and policy overview essay ('Letter') outlining three stylized phases of municipal water and sanitation development and proposing a four-component policy mix for utilities in the Anthropocene. While Sections 2 and 4 discuss tariff and cost-recovery rules (increasing block tariffs, subsidies, Customer Assistance Programs), utility regulation and informal 'shadow state' governance, those sections present narrative commentary citing prior literature without primary data, an empirical study design or a systematic empirical synthesis (E05). Section 3 presents six illustrative cross-country bivariate scatterplots from IBNET and GWI (without a methods section or reported sample sizes), but its service-access plots (Figures 1-3: piped water, sewer connections and wastewater treatment) examine only national GDP per capita rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory or tariff factor, and its tariff/cost-recovery plots (Figures 4-6: OCCR, revenue per m3 and price for 15 m3) examine only GDP per capita and hydrological water stress without measuring any service-access outcome. Accordingly, the paper is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Conceptual framework and policy overview essay with illustrative descriptive cross-country scatterplots from secondary databases (IBNET and GWI)
